claim: Genes encoding dpr and DIP immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF) members are expressed in fru P1 neurons.
source: A reanalysis of genomic studies shows that genes encoding dpr and DIP immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF) members are expressed in fru P1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by reanalysis of genomic studies as stated in the abstract and detailed in the manuscript.

claim: Each fru P1 and dpr/DIP (fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP) overlapping expression pattern is similar in both sexes.
source: We find that each fru P1 and dpr/DIP (fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP) overlapping expression pattern is similar in both sexes, but there are dimorphisms in neuronal morphology and cell number.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from immunofluorescence analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are dimorphisms in neuronal morphology and cell number in fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP neurons between sexes.
source: We find that each fru P1 and dpr/DIP (fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP) overlapping expression pattern is similar in both sexes, but there are dimorphisms in neuronal morphology and cell number.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from immunofluorescence analyses and quantification presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mushroom body functions together with the lateral protocerebral complex to direct courtship behavior.
source: Behavioral studies of fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP perturbation genotypes indicate that the mushroom body functions together with the lateral protocerebral complex to direct courtship behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral studies using neuronal activation and silencing experiments.

claim: Many DIPs have high expression in a small set of neurons.
source: A single-cell RNA-seq analysis of fru P1 neurons shows that many DIPs have high expression in a small set of neurons, whereas the dprs are often expressed in a larger set of neurons at intermediate levels, with a myriad of dpr/DIP expression combinations.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dprs are often expressed in a larger set of neurons at intermediate levels.
source: A single-cell RNA-seq analysis of fru P1 neurons shows that many DIPs have high expression in a small set of neurons, whereas the dprs are often expressed in a larger set of neurons at intermediate levels, with a myriad of dpr/DIP expression combinations.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Perturbations of sex hierarchy genes change the sex-specific morphologies of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons.
source: Functionally, we find that perturbations of sex hierarchy genes and of DIP-ε change the sex-specific morphologies of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Perturbations of DIP-ε change the sex-specific morphologies of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons.
source: Functionally, we find that perturbations of sex hierarchy genes and of DIP-ε change the sex-specific morphologies of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Drosophila reproductive behaviors are directed by fruitless neurons.
source: Drosophila reproductive behaviors are directed by fruitless neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Small subsets of neurons have been identified as critical for all aspects of reproductive behaviors.
source: Small subsets of neurons have been identified as critical for all aspects of reproductive behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: These neurons express sex-specific transcription factors encoded by doublesex (dsx) and fruitless (fru; fru P1 transcripts are spliced under sex hierarchy regulation; Figure 1A) (reviewed in Dauwalder, 2011; Yamamoto et al., 2014; Andrew et al., 2019; Leitner and Ben-Shahar, 2020).
source: These neurons express sex-specific transcription factors encoded by doublesex (dsx) and fruitless (fru; fru P1 transcripts are spliced under sex hierarchy regulation; Figure 1A) (reviewed in Dauwalder, 2011; Yamamoto et al., 2014; Andrew et al., 2019; Leitner and Ben-Shahar, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: dsx- and fru P1-expressing neurons are present in males and females in similar positions.
source: dsx- and fru P1-expressing neurons are present in males and females in similar positions, and arise through a shared developmental trajectory (Ren et al., 2016), although these neurons direct very different behaviors in males and females.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ren et al., 2016.

claim: dsx- and fru P1-expressing neurons arise through a shared developmental trajectory.
source: dsx- and fru P1-expressing neurons are present in males and females in similar positions, and arise through a shared developmental trajectory (Ren et al., 2016), although these neurons direct very different behaviors in males and females.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ren et al., 2016.

claim: dsx- and fru P1-expressing neurons direct very different behaviors in males and females.
source: dsx- and fru P1-expressing neurons are present in males and females in similar positions, and arise through a shared developmental trajectory (Ren et al., 2016), although these neurons direct very different behaviors in males and females.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Males display an elaborate courtship ritual that includes chasing the female, tapping her with his leg, and production of song with wing vibration.
source: Males display an elaborate courtship ritual that includes chasing the female, tapping her with his leg, and production of song with wing vibration (reviewed in Greenspan and Ferveur, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The female decides whether she will mate.
source: The female decides whether she will mate and then, if mated, displays post-mating behaviors that include egg laying, changes in diet, and changes in receptivity to courtship (see Laturney and Billeter, 2014; Aranha and Vasconcelos, 2018; Newell et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: If mated, females display post-mating behaviors that include egg laying, changes in diet, and changes in receptivity to courtship.
source: The female decides whether she will mate and then, if mated, displays post-mating behaviors that include egg laying, changes in diet, and changes in receptivity to courtship (see Laturney and Billeter, 2014; Aranha and Vasconcelos, 2018; Newell et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The presence of two X chromosomes in females results in splicing of Sxl pre-mRNA, such that functional Sxl is produced.
source: The presence of two X chromosomes in females results in splicing of Sxl pre-mRNA, such that functional Sxl is produced.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the Drosophila sex determination hierarchy.

claim: Sxl regulates Sxl and tra pre-mRNA splicing, resulting in continued production of functional Sxl and Tra in females.
source: Sxl regulates Sxl and tra pre-mRNA splicing, resulting in continued production of functional Sxl and Tra in females.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the Drosophila sex determination hierarchy.

claim: Tra and Tra-2 regulate the pre-mRNA splicing of dsx and fru P1 in females.
source: Tra and Tra-2 regulate the pre-mRNA splicing of dsx and fru P1 in females, whereas in males dsx and fru P1 are spliced by the default pre-mRNA splicing pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the Drosophila sex determination hierarchy.

claim: In males dsx and fru P1 are spliced by the default pre-mRNA splicing pathway.
source: Tra and Tra-2 regulate the pre-mRNA splicing of dsx and fru P1 in females, whereas in males dsx and fru P1 are spliced by the default pre-mRNA splicing pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the Drosophila sex determination hierarchy.

claim: The sex-specific splicing results in production of sex-specific Dsx and Fru transcription factors.
source: The sex-specific splicing results in production of sex-specific Dsx and Fru transcription factors (Burtis and Baker, 1989; Ito et al., 1996; Ryner et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: dsx regulates sex differences that lead to both dimorphic behavior and gross anatomical morphological differences.
source: dsx regulates sex differences that lead to both dimorphic behavior and gross anatomical morphological differences, whereas fru P1 regulates sex differences that lead to dimorphic behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: fru P1 regulates sex differences that lead to dimorphic behaviors.
source: dsx regulates sex differences that lead to both dimorphic behavior and gross anatomical morphological differences, whereas fru P1 regulates sex differences that lead to dimorphic behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Previous genome-wide studies found that dpr/DIPs are regulated downstream of fru P1, FruM, and/or are expressed in fru P1 neurons.
source: Previous genome-wide studies found that dpr/DIPs are regulated downstream of fru P1, FruM, and/or are expressed in fru P1 neurons (Goldman and Arbeitman, 2007; Dalton et al., 2013; Neville et al., 2014; Vernes, 2015; Newell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple genome-wide studies and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Sex differences in the nervous system that contribute to reproductive behaviors include dimorphism in dsx and fru P1 neuron number, connectivity, and physiology.
source: Sex differences in the nervous system that contribute to reproductive behaviors include dimorphism in dsx and fru P1 neuron number, connectivity, and physiology.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Several genome-wide studies have been performed to find genes that are regulated by male-specific Fru (FruM) or are expressed in fru P1 neurons.
source: Several genome-wide studies have been performed to find genes that are regulated by male-specific Fru (FruM) or are expressed in fru P1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple genome-wide studies.

claim: These independent studies examined fru P1 loss-of-function and gain-of-function gene expression changes, fru P1 cell-type-specific gene expression, and the direct targets for FruM binding.
source: These independent studies examined fru P1 loss-of-function and gain-of-function gene expression changes, fru P1 cell-type-specific gene expression, and the direct targets for FruM binding (Goldman and Arbeitman, 2007; Dalton et al., 2013; Neville et al., 2014; Vernes, 2015; Newell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple genome-wide studies.

claim: The Dpr and DIP proteins are membrane-linked cell adhesion molecules with N-terminal extracellular Ig domains and C-terminal glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI) linkage sequences or transmembrane domains.
source: The Dpr and DIP proteins are membrane-linked cell adhesion molecules with N-terminal extracellular Ig domains and C-terminal glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI) linkage sequences or transmembrane domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Dpr and DIP protein structure.

claim: The Dpr proteins have two extracellular Ig domains.
source: The Dpr proteins have two extracellular Ig domains, whereas DIPs have three (reviewed in Zinn and Özkan, 2017; Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: DIPs have three extracellular Ig domains.
source: The Dpr proteins have two extracellular Ig domains, whereas DIPs have three (reviewed in Zinn and Özkan, 2017; Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: dpr1 has a role in gating the timing of the male courtship steps.
source: In addition to the genomic studies, our previous work showed that dpr1, the founding member of the dpr family (Nakamura et al., 2002), has a role in gating the timing of the male courtship steps (Goldman and Arbeitman, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: There are sex-differences in arborization volumes throughout the central nervous system.
source: The finding that cell adhesion molecules are regulated by FruM fits well with studies that showed that there are sex-differences in arborization volumes throughout the central nervous system (Cachero et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Differences in neuronal connectivity are one mechanism to generate behavioral dimorphism.
source: Thus, it was predicted that differences in neuronal connectivity are one mechanism to generate behavioral dimorphism (Cachero et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature and represents a prediction based on previous findings.

claim: Most DIPs interact with multiple Dprs, and vice versa.
source: In-depth, in vitro analyses of Dpr/DIP protein-protein interactions have shown that most DIPs interact with multiple Dprs, and vice versa.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro protein-protein interaction studies.

claim: 4 of the 11 DIPs display homophilic interactions.
source: Additionally, 4 of the 11 DIPs and 2 of the 21 Dprs display homophilic interactions, and there are two heterophilic interactions between Dprs (Özkan et al., 2013; Carrillo et al., 2015; Cosmanescu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: 2 of the 21 Dprs display homophilic interactions.
source: Additionally, 4 of the 11 DIPs and 2 of the 21 Dprs display homophilic interactions, and there are two heterophilic interactions between Dprs (Özkan et al., 2013; Carrillo et al., 2015; Cosmanescu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: There are two heterophilic interactions between Dprs.
source: Additionally, 4 of the 11 DIPs and 2 of the 21 Dprs display homophilic interactions, and there are two heterophilic interactions between Dprs (Özkan et al., 2013; Carrillo et al., 2015; Cosmanescu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Functional analyses of the Dprs and DIPs have revealed roles in synaptic connectivity and specificity of neuronal targeting in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, visual system, and olfactory system.
source: Functional analyses of the Dprs and DIPs have revealed roles in synaptic connectivity and specificity of neuronal targeting in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, visual system, and olfactory system (Carrillo et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2015; Barish et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018; Ashley et al., 2019; Courgeon and Desplan, 2019; Menon et al., 2019; Venkatasubramanian et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple functional studies.

claim: Cell adhesion molecules have been shown to be important for sculpting dimorphism in fru P1 neurons.
source: Additionally, cell adhesion molecules have already been shown to be important for sculpting dimorphism in fru P1 neurons, with studies of the IgSF member encoded by roundabout (robo) shown to be a direct target of FruM and responsible for dimorphic projections and morphology (Mellert et al., 2010; Ito et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: roundabout (robo) is a direct target of FruM and responsible for dimorphic projections and morphology.
source: Additionally, cell adhesion molecules have already been shown to be important for sculpting dimorphism in fru P1 neurons, with studies of the IgSF member encoded by roundabout (robo) shown to be a direct target of FruM and responsible for dimorphic projections and morphology (Mellert et al., 2010; Ito et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The majority of the dpr/DIP genes are identified as regulated by FruM or expressed in fru P1 neurons in at least three of the independent genome-wide studies.
source: The majority of the dpr/DIP genes are identified as regulated by FruM or expressed in fru P1 neurons in at least three of these independent genome-wide studies (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reanalysis of genomic data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: FruM binding sites were found near/in all but two dpr/DIP loci that are examined.
source: When we search for the presence of the three DNA sequence motifs near/in the dpr/DIP loci, FruM binding sites were found near/in all but two dpr/DIP loci that are examined (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational DNA-binding site analysis.

claim: Live-tissue staining revealed sexual dimorphism in binding of tagged Dpr/DIP proteins to fru P1 neurons in the subesophageal ganglion brain region, with more neurons with overlap detected in males.
source: Further evidence that dprs/DIPs have a role in fru P1 neurons comes from a live-tissue staining approach, using epitope-tagged, extracellular regions of a Dpr or DIP to examine binding (as done in Fox and Zinn, 2005; Lee et al., 2009; Özkan et al., 2013). This revealed sexual dimorphism in binding of tagged Dpr/DIP proteins to fru P1 neurons in the subesophageal ganglion brain region, with more neurons with overlap detected in males (Brovero et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a live-tissue staining study.

claim: Every dpr and DIP gene is either regulated by FruM or expressed in fru P1 neurons in either males and females.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that every dpr and DIP gene is either regulated by FruM or expressed in fru P1 neurons in either males and females.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including genomic studies, computational analysis, and live-tissue staining.

claim: 24 genotypes showed clear and consistent, membrane-bound GFP expression in the central nervous system.
source: Based on our examination of the expression patterns in 27 intersecting genotypes, we find that 24 genotypes showed clear and consistent, membrane-bound GFP expression in the central nervous system.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses of fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP genotypes.

claim: Only two fru P1 ∩ DIP genotypes have restricted and unique patterns (fru P1 ∩ DIP-δ and fru P1 ∩ DIP-α).
source: Of these, only two fru P1 ∩ DIP genotypes have restricted and unique patterns (fru P1 ∩ DIP-δ and fru P1 ∩ DIP-α), whereas the other genotypes have broader expression, with many in similar regions/patterns (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The 22 intersecting genotypes with broad expression, in both males and females, have consistent expression in the brain lateral protocerebral complex, including within the arch, ring, junction, and crescent.
source: The 22 intersecting genotypes with broad expression, in both males and females, have consistent expression in the brain lateral protocerebral complex, including within the arch, ring, junction, and crescent (for summary see Figure 7 and Source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 7 and Source data 1.

claim: The lateral protocerebral complex has been shown to have fru P1 neurons with sexually dimorphic arbor volumes.
source: This region has been shown to have fru P1 neurons with sexually dimorphic arbor volumes (Cachero et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The lateral protocerebral complex has inputs from sensory neurons and is predicted to be a site of sensory integration, to direct motor output necessary for coordinating courtship activity.
source: Furthermore, the lateral protocerebral complex has inputs from sensory neurons and is predicted to be a site of sensory integration, to direct motor output necessary for coordinating courtship activity (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to relevant literature and represents a prediction.

claim: Eight intersecting genotypes have expression in mushroom bodies in both males and females.
source: We find eight intersecting genotypes have expression in mushroom bodies in both males and females.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: The mushroom body region has a well-established role in learning and memory, including learning in the context of courtship rejection.
source: This region has a well-established role in learning and memory, including learning in the context of courtship rejection (Jones et al., 2018; McBride et al., 1999; Montague and Baker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The majority of fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP genotypes have expression in similar regions, suggesting that some may function in a combinatorial manner within a neuron to direct patterning and/or synaptic targeting.
source: Overall, the majority of fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP genotypes have expression in similar regions, suggesting that some may function in a combinatorial manner within a neuron to direct patterning and/or synaptic targeting, consistent with the single-cell RNA-sequencing data presented below.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and inference from expression patterns.

claim: 18 intersecting genotypes show consistent presence of signal in the mesothoracic triangle neuronal projections in males, but only two genotypes do so in females.
source: For example, 18 intersecting genotypes show consistent presence of signal in the mesothoracic triangle neuronal projections in males, but only two genotypes do so in females.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Both males and female have expression in the DA1 and VA1v antennal lobe glomeruli in several intersecting genotypes.
source: While both males and female have expression in the DA1 and VA1v antennal lobe glomeruli in several intersecting genotypes, we also observe sexual dimorphism, with four genotypes having consistent expression in only female DA1 glomeruli (fru P1 ∩ dpr3, dpr10, dpr17, DIP-θ).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Four genotypes have consistent expression in only female DA1 glomeruli (fru P1 ∩ dpr3, dpr10, dpr17, DIP-θ).
source: While both males and female have expression in the DA1 and VA1v antennal lobe glomeruli in several intersecting genotypes, we also observe sexual dimorphism, with four genotypes having consistent expression in only female DA1 glomeruli (fru P1 ∩ dpr3, dpr10, dpr17, DIP-θ).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: In the ventral nerve cord, neurons that cross the midline are consistently observed only in males and not females.
source: In the ventral nerve cord, neurons that cross the midline are consistently observed only in males and not females.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Previous work found a midline crossing phenotype that was also male-specific for a set of gustatory neurons.
source: Previous work found a midline crossing phenotype that was also male-specific for a set of gustatory neurons (Mellert et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to relevant literature.

claim: For all regions where cell bodies are counted, the trend was that there are more cell bodies in males than females.
source: For all regions where cell bodies are counted, the trend was that there are more cell bodies in males than females.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell bodies from immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: The differences in the patterns of expression between males and females are not large, with several genotypes having quantitative differences in the numbers of cell bodies present.
source: Thus, the differences in the patterns of expression between males and females are not large, with several genotypes having quantitative differences in the numbers of cell bodies present.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell bodies from immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Neuronal activation resulted in decreases in male following and wing extending toward females for several genotypes.
source: We find that neuronal activation resulted in decreases in male following and wing extending toward females for several genotypes (Figure 4 and Source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TrpA1 activation and reference to Figure 4 and Source data 2.

claim: Neuronal activation of fru P1 ∩ dpr (13 of 16) and fru P1 ∩ DIP (2 of 8) genotypes caused atypical courtship behavior toward a female, including double wing extension, and continuous abdominal bending.
source: We also observe that neuronal activation of fru P1 ∩ dpr (13 of 16) and fru P1 ∩ DIP (2 of 8) genotypes caused atypical courtship behavior toward a female, including double wing extension, and continuous abdominal bending, even if the female had moved away (Figures 4 and 7; for abdominal bending phenotype see Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TrpA1 activation and reference to Figures 4 and 7.

claim: Some males ejaculated on the chamber in five intersecting genotypes: dpr5 (5 of 15 animals), dpr9 (3 of 15 animals), dpr10 (3 of 15 animals), dpr12 (2 of 15 animals), and DIP-θ (4 of 15 animals).
source: Additionally, we found that some males ejaculated on the chamber in five intersecting genotypes: dpr5 (5 of 15 animals), dpr9 (3 of 15 animals), dpr10 (3 of 15 animals), dpr12 (2 of 15 animals), and DIP-θ (4 of 15 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TrpA1 activation.

claim: fru P1 ∩ DIP-α is the only strain that showed a decrease in courtship activities without a concomitant increase in atypical courtship behaviors.
source: Of note, fru P1 ∩ DIP-α is the only strain that showed a decrease in courtship activities without a concomitant increase in atypical courtship behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TrpA1 activation.

claim: fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons may normally inhibit courtship behaviors when they are activated.
source: This suggests that fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons may normally inhibit courtship behaviors when they are activated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral assay results.

claim: Activation of the fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP neurons is sufficient to elicit single wing extension, double wing extension, and abdominal bending in fru P1 ∩ dprs (11 of 16 genotypes) and fru P1 ∩ DIPs (3 of 8 genotypes) in solitary males.
source: We find that activation of the fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP neurons is sufficient to elicit single wing extension, double wing extension, and abdominal bending in fru P1 ∩ dprs (11 of 16 genotypes) and fru P1 ∩ DIPs (3 of 8 genotypes) (Figures 5 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TrpA1 activation in solitary males and reference to Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Activating the intersecting fru P1 neuronal populations of fru P1 ∩ dpr5 (5 of 10 animals), dpr9 (1 of 10 animals), dpr10 (1 of 10 animals), dpr12 (3 of 10 animals), and DIP-θ (1of 10 animals) causes males to ejaculate without a female present.
source: Similarly, activating the intersecting fru P1 neuronal populations of fru P1 ∩ dpr5 (5 of 10 animals), dpr9 (1 of 10 animals), dpr10 (1 of 10 animals), dpr12 (3 of 10 animals), and DIP-θ (1of 10 animals) causes males to ejaculate without a female present.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TrpA1 activation in solitary males.

claim: Activation of these subsets of fru P1 neurons is sufficient to direct reproductive behaviors, even if a female is not present.
source: Overall, activation of these subsets of fru P1 neurons is sufficient to direct reproductive behaviors, even if a female is not present, consistent with other neuronal activation experiments (reviewed in Auer and Benton, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TrpA1 activation in solitary males and citation to a review article.

claim: Silencing fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP neuronal subsets in several genotypes resulted in motor defects.
source: Given that neuronal silencing in several genotypes resulted in motor defects, in which the male fell and was unable to quickly right himself (p<0.005 for strong motor defects; 0.05>p>0.005 for minor motor defects in Figure 6), we quantify the time when the fly could not right himself as 'motor defect' and subtracted this from the overall courtship time for behavioral indices (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TNT silencing and reference to Figure 6.

claim: The intersecting genotypes that consistently demonstrate motor defects additionally show decreases in following and wing extension upon silencing (fru P1 ∩ dpr1, dpr3, dpr4, dpr5, dpr9, dpr10, dpr11, dpr12, dpr15, and DIP-η).
source: The intersecting genotypes that consistently demonstrate motor defects additionally show decreases in following and wing extension upon silencing, likely due to some motor defect (fru P1 ∩ dpr1, dpr3, dpr4, dpr5, dpr9, dpr10, dpr11, dpr12, dpr15, and DIP-η).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TNT silencing.

claim: Seven intersecting genotypes had a decrease in following/wing extension indices and only minor or no motor defect (fru P1 ∩ dpr2, dpr6, dpr17, dpr18, DIP-ε, DIP-θ, and DIP-γ).
source: However, seven intersecting genotypes had a decrease in following/wing extension indices and only minor or no motor defect (fru P1 ∩ dpr2, dpr6, dpr17, dpr18, DIP-ε, DIP-θ, and DIP-γ).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TNT silencing.

claim: One genotype, fru P1 ∩ dpr7, has an increase in following/wing extension with neuronal silencing.
source: One genotype, fru P1 ∩ dpr7, has an increase in following/wing extension with neuronal silencing.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TNT silencing.

claim: In the case of fru P1 ∩ dpr7, we do not detect GFP expression in the central or peripheral nervous system in adults.
source: In the case of fru P1 ∩ dpr7, we do not detect GFP expression in the central or peripheral nervous system in adults, so the neurons underlying this phenotype remain to be determined.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: If there is a significant difference in the DAM assay, the intersecting genotype with neuronal silencing has increased locomotor activity.
source: If there is a significant difference, the intersecting genotype with neuronal silencing has increased locomotor activity in the DAM assay, suggesting that the courtship phenotypes are not due to overall loss in locomotor activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by Drosophila Activity Monitor (DAM) assays.

claim: Silencing fru P1 ∩ dprs (13 of 17 genotypes) is more likely to cause a courtship defect than silencing fru P1 ∩ DIPs (4 of 9 genotypes).
source: As above in the neuronal activating experiments, silencing fru P1 ∩ dprs (13 of 17 genotypes) is more likely to cause a courtship defect than silencing fru P1 ∩ DIPs (4 of 9 genotypes).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TNT silencing.

claim: Silencing fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP neurons in the central nervous system, for most genotypes, suppresses courtship.
source: Given the large effect size of the courtship defects compared to the smaller effect size of the motor defect, it is clear that silencing fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP neurons in the central nervous system, for most genotypes, suppresses courtship (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TNT silencing and reference to Figure 6.

claim: Silencing fru P1 neurons in males leads to decreased courtship toward a female.
source: This is consistent with previous studies that have found that silencing fru P1 neurons in males leads to decreased courtship toward a female (Manoli et al., 2005; Stockinger et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: fru P1 ∩ DIP-α is the only strain to demonstrate motor defects, but no change in courtship behaviors upon silencing.
source: Interestingly, fru P1 ∩ DIP-α is the only strain to demonstrate motor defects, but no change in courtship behaviors upon silencing, underscoring the previous hypothesis that these neurons may normally be inhibitory for courtship.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays using TNT silencing.

claim: There is a set of eight intersecting genotypes grouped together that all have expression in the mushroom body and several regions within the lateral protocerebral complex.
source: There is a set of eight intersecting genotypes grouped together on the right of the dendrogram that all have expression in the mushroom body and several regions within the lateral protocerebral complex, but varied expression across the other morphological features (Figure 7A; fru P1 ∩ dpr4, dpr5, dpr8, dpr9, dpr10, dpr12, dpr14, and DIP-γ).
evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis of expression data and reference to Figure 7A.

claim: Seven of the eight intersecting genotypes with mushroom body and lateral protocerebral complex expression have similar types of atypical courtship behaviors in the activating experiments (excluding fru P1 ∩ dpr8).
source: Seven have similar types of atypical courtship behaviors in the activating experiments (excluding fru P1 ∩ dpr8), in the male-female courtship assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Not all intersecting genotypes with expression in the abdominal ganglion show the ejaculation phenotype.
source: However, not all intersecting genotypes with expression in the abdominal ganglion show the ejaculation phenotype, even those with a relatively high number of neuronal cell body counts in the abdominal ganglion (see fru P1 ∩ dpr1 and dpr2), suggesting that it is the combination of neurons that are activated that is critical for this phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis of expression and behavioral data.

claim: There is an intersecting genotype that does not have mushroom body expression, but also has the ejaculation phenotype (fru P1 ∩ DIP-θ).
source: Furthermore, there is an intersecting genotype that does not have mushroom body expression, but also has the ejaculation phenotype (fru P1 ∩ DIP-θ).
evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis of expression and behavioral data.

claim: The results point to a critical role for interactions between the mushroom body and protocerebral complex in directing courtship behaviors.
source: Overall, the results point to a critical role for interactions between the mushroom body and protocerebral complex in directing courtship behaviors, which are modified by being activated in combination with other neuronal populations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from meta-analysis of expression and behavioral data.

claim: Connections between the mushroom body and protocerebral complex may integrate diverse external stimuli with internal physiological state and previous behavioral experience.
source: This is consistent with an idea put forth previously that posited connections between these two brain regions may integrate diverse external stimuli with internal physiological state and previous behavioral experience (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to relevant literature and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Twenty-two intersecting genotypes have expression in different regions of lateral protocerebral complex, but no consistent expression in the mushroom body.
source: Twenty-two intersecting genotypes have expression in different regions of lateral protocerebral complex, but no consistent expression in the mushroom body.
evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis of expression data.

claim: An examination of the behavioral data reveals no phenotypes correlated with the lateral protocerebral complex expression data.
source: An examination of the behavioral data reveals no phenotypes correlated with the lateral protocerebral complex expression data.
evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis of expression and behavioral data.

claim: Interactions across different combinations of activated neurons, in each intersecting genotype, are critical for the behavioral outcomes.
source: While the lateral protocerebral complex is critical for higher order processing, the data further supports the idea that interactions across different combinations of activated neurons, in each intersecting genotype, are critical for the behavioral outcomes and underscores how different patterns of neuronal activity can direct similar behavioral outcomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from meta-analysis of expression and behavioral data.

claim: Some Dprs with the same DIP interacting partners have the most similar expression patterns.
source: It appears that some Dprs/DIPs that bind the same partner have the most similar expression patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of expression data.

claim: In both males and females fru P1 neurons may express a reporter for both a DIP and a dpr that can bind to it.
source: Therefore, in both males and females, fru P1 neurons may express a reporter for both a DIP and a dpr that can bind to it.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis of expression data.

claim: In both males and females fru P1 ∩ dpr11 has correlated expression with fru P1 ∩ dpr1 and dpr2, but Dpr11 interacts with DIPs that Dpr1, and Dpr2 do not interact with.
source: In both males and females fru P1 ∩ dpr11 has correlated expression with fru P1 ∩ dpr1 and dpr2, but Dpr11 interacts with DIPs that Dpr1, and Dpr2 do not interact with.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of expression data and known protein-protein interactions.

claim: Expression of different combinations of Dprs that interact with different DIPs is a mechanism used to direct the specificity and strength of interactions.
source: This suggests that expression of different combinations of Dprs that interact with different DIPs is a mechanism used to direct the specificity and strength of interactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis of expression data.

claim: fru P1 ∩ DIP-α and DIP-δ have the most restricted expression patterns and they are not highly correlated with the expression patterns of their interacting Dpr partners, in either males or females.
source: fru P1 ∩ DIP-α and DIP-δ have the most restricted expression patterns and they are not highly correlated with the expression patterns of their interacting Dpr partners, in either males or females.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of expression data.

claim: Reporters for Dprs that bind the same DIP can be expressed in the same neurons, as well as in different neurons.
source: Consistent with the single-cell RNA-seq analysis (below), these data show that reporters for Dprs that bind the same DIP can be expressed in the same neurons, as well as in different neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of expression data and single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Some Dprs with different binding partners have correlated expression, which could be a mechanism to mediate the specificity and strength of neuronal adhesion.
source: Additionally, some Dprs with different binding partners have correlated expression, which could be a mechanism to mediate the specificity and strength of neuronal adhesion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis of expression data.

claim: All fru P1 neurons express at least one dpr/DIP.
source: We find that all fru P1 neurons express at least one dpr/DIP.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The patterns of dpr/DIP expression are not distinct enough to generate clusters that have large separation in the UMAP plot.
source: A visual inspection of the UMAP plot reveals that the patterns of dpr/DIP expression are not distinct enough to generate clusters that have large separation in the UMAP plot.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and UMAP visualization.

claim: Previous single-cell RNA-seq studies from adult central nervous system tissues found that dprs/DIPs are cell identity marker genes.
source: We note that previous single-cell RNA-seq studies from adult central nervous system tissues found that dprs/DIPs are cell identity marker genes (Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Allen et al., 2020), with higher, enriched expression in subsets of neurons, rather than pan-neuronal expression, consistent with our results.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous single-cell RNA-seq studies.

claim: The UMAP clustering patterning is not due to co-expression of Dpr/DIP interacting partners.
source: The UMAP clustering patterning is not due to co-expression of Dpr/DIP interacting partners (Figure 8C), based on a visual inspection, which might be expected if Dprs/DIPs predominantly interact in cis.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and visual inspection of UMAP plot.

claim: The majority of the DIPs have high average expression in one cluster, with a large percent of the cells in the cluster having expression.
source: We find that the majority of the DIPs have high average expression in one cluster, with a large percent of the cells in the cluster having expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The majority of the dprs have moderate average expression and the percent of cells that express the dpr is similar across many clusters.
source: This is distinct from the majority of the dprs, where the average expression and the percent of cells that express the dpr is moderate and similar across many clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The DIPs have more restricted expression compared to dprs.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of the expression patterns overlaid on the UMAP plot for each dpr/DIP shows that the DIPs have more restricted expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and UMAP visualization.

claim: dpr21 is broadly detected across the UMAP plot.
source: For example, dpr21 is broadly detected across the UMAP plot, whereas DIP-α has restricted expression in cluster 10, at the upper left-hand side of the UMAP plot (subset of expression patterns in Figure 8D; for all dprs/DIPs see Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and UMAP visualization.

claim: DIP-α has restricted expression in cluster 10, at the upper left-hand side of the UMAP plot.
source: For example, dpr21 is broadly detected across the UMAP plot, whereas DIP-α has restricted expression in cluster 10, at the upper left-hand side of the UMAP plot (subset of expression patterns in Figure 8D; for all dprs/DIPs see Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and UMAP visualization.

claim: This observation is consistent with cell-type-specific RNA-seq data from the Drosophila visual system, where the DIPs were among the most specifically expressed genes and dprs were more broadly expressed.
source: This observation is consistent with cell-type-specific RNA-seq data from the Drosophila visual system (Tan et al., 2015; Cosmanescu et al., 2018; Davis et al., 2020), where the DIPs were among the most specifically expressed genes and dprs were more broadly expressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to cell-type-specific RNA-seq studies.

claim: DIPs may have different functional roles, compared to Dprs, in terms of directing synaptic specificity or cell adhesion properties of the neuron.
source: This suggests that DIPs may have different functional roles, compared to Dprs, in terms of directing synaptic specificity or cell adhesion properties of the neuron.
evidence: The claim is inferred from single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Some dprs and DIPs that have shared interacting partners have the most similar expression to each other.
source: We find that some dprs and DIPs that have shared interacting partners have the most similar expression to each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: The following pairs have the most similar expression patterns: dpr2 and dpr3; dpr6 and dpr10; dpr16 and dpr17; and DIP-ζ and DIP-ε.
source: This includes the following pairs: dpr2 and dpr3; dpr6 and dpr10; dpr16 and dpr17; and DIP-ζ and DIP-ε.
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: DIP-α, and DIP-ι have the most distinct expression patterns from the rest of the interactome.
source: We find that DIP-α, and DIP-ι have the most distinct expression patterns from the rest of the interactome, which may be due to the low number of cells in which they are detected (see Upset plot described below; Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: For some neurons, co-expression of dprs and DIPs with the same interacting partners may be a mechanism to generate different adhesion properties.
source: For some neurons, co-expression of dprs and DIPs with the same interacting partners may be a mechanism to generate different adhesion properties, as noted above.
evidence: The claim is inferred from single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: There are 458 neurons that express only one dpr or DIP.
source: There are 458 neurons that express only one dpr or DIP.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The range of neurons that express 2–8 dprs and DIPs is between 451–653 neurons (4024 neurons total).
source: The range of neurons that express 2–8 dprs and DIPs is between 451–653 neurons (4024 neurons total); that express 9–11 dprs and DIPs is between 105–332 neurons (657 neurons total); and that express 12–15 dprs and DIPs is between 5–45 neurons (79 neurons total; Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The majority of expression repertoires that are detected in more than one neuron are those for which the neuron only expresses one dpr or DIP (457 neurons).
source: The majority of expression repertoires that are detected in more than one neuron are those for which the neuron only expresses one dpr or DIP (single dots on bottom of Upset Plot, 457 neurons; Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and Upset plot analysis.

claim: There were also 466 neurons that had shared co-expression combinations due to expression of 2–5 dprs and DIPs.
source: There were also 466 neurons that had shared co-expression combinations due to expression of 2–5 dprs and DIPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and Upset plot analysis.

claim: The majority of fru P1 neurons had a unique repertoire of dpr/DIP expression (4295 neurons), due to expression of different combinations of 2–15 dprs and DIPs.
source: The majority of fru P1 neurons had a unique repertoire of dpr/DIP expression (4295 neurons), due to expression of different combinations of 2–15 dprs and DIPs (Source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis and Upset plot analysis.

claim: In developing fru P1 neurons, this range of expression patterns of the dprs and DIPs may provide a mechanism to generate different connectivity properties for each neuron.
source: In developing fru P1 neurons, this range of expression patterns of the dprs and DIPs may provide a mechanism to generate different connectivity properties for each neuron.
evidence: The claim is inferred from single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons are sexually dimorphic.
source: After examining all the fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP patterns, and the single-cell RNA-seq data, it became apparent that fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons are sexually dimorphic, and that this is one of the genotypes with the fewest cells among the genotypes that were scored (Source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: fru P1 ∩ DIP-α is one of the genotypes with the fewest cells among the genotypes that were scored.
source: After examining all the fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP patterns, and the single-cell RNA-seq data, it became apparent that fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons are sexually dimorphic, and that this is one of the genotypes with the fewest cells among the genotypes that were scored (Source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell bodies from immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: There are sex-differences in the superior medial protocerebrum region (SMP), where females have a longer and broader projection, as compared to males.
source: There are sex-differences in the superior medial protocerebrum region (SMP; Figure 9A and B, subpanels I), where females have a longer (dotted-line) and broader projection (arrowhead), as compared to males.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 9.

claim: In the medial part of the midbrain, an 'M' shaped peak forms ('M'-like) in males that is not typically observed in females.
source: Moreover, in the medial part of the midbrain, an 'M' shaped peak forms ('M'-like) in males that is not typically observed in females (curved dotted-line, Figure 9A and B, subpanels II and III).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 9.

claim: In the ventral lateral protocerebrum region (VLP) there are neuronal cell bodies and projections in a 'square' shaped pattern that are more frequently observed in females.
source: Additionally, in the ventral lateral protocerebrum region (VLP) there are neuronal cell bodies (arrowhead, Figure 9A and B, subpanels II and III), and projections in a 'square' shaped pattern that are more frequently observed in females (closed dotted-line, Figure 9A and B, subpanels II and III).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 9.

claim: There is a greater frequency of neuronal cell bodies present in the subesophageal ganglion (SEG) in females, as compared to males.
source: There is also a greater frequency of neuronal cell bodies present in the subesophageal ganglion (SEG) in females, as compared to males (arrowhead, Figure 9A and B, subpanels IV).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 9.

claim: In the abdominal ganglia (AbG) of the ventral nerve cord there is a higher density of projections in males.
source: In the abdominal ganglia (AbG) of the ventral nerve cord there is a higher density of projections in males (Figure 9A and B, subpanels V).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 9.

claim: Females have a distinct 'forceps' shaped pattern in the AbG region.
source: In contrast, females have a distinct 'forceps' shaped pattern in the AbG region (arrowhead, Figure 9A and B, subpanels V).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 9.

claim: The sex differences in fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons are due to differences in the number of neurons and also in the morphology of projections and arborizations.
source: Taken together, it appears that the sex differences are due to differences in the number of neurons and also in the morphology of projections and arborizations (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 9.

claim: In males, overexpression of TraF causes the projections in the SMP to become more female-like.
source: In males, the projections in the SMP became more female-like (Figure 9C–D, subpanels I).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: In males, overexpression of TraF causes the horizontal projections in the medial part of midbrain to be either more female-like or not detected in half of the male samples.
source: In the medial part of midbrain, the horizontal projections in half of the male samples were either more female-like or not detected (Figure 9C–D, subpanels II).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: In males, overexpression of TraF causes the neuronal patterns within the AbG to be either more female-like or absent in half of the male samples.
source: Similarly, among half of the male samples, the neuronal patterns within the AbG are either more female-like or absent (Figure 9C–D, subpanels V).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Overexpressing TraF in females produces unexpected phenotypes, suggesting that quantitative differences in TraF have biological outcomes.
source: We observed unexpected phenotypes in females upon overexpressing TraF, which suggests that quantitative differences in TraF have biological outcomes, as we previously suggested (Arbeitman et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and citation to previous work.

claim: In females, overexpression of TraF causes a lateral ascending neuronal projection to be observed more frequently in the VLP region.
source: For instance, a lateral ascending neuronal projection was observed more frequently in the VLP region (Figure 9C–D, subpanels III dotted line).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: In females, overexpression of TraF causes the neuronal cell bodies in the VLP, the adjacent 'square' shaped projection patterns and the medial horizontal projection to be less frequently observed, as compared to control females.
source: However, the neuronal cell bodies in the VLP, the adjacent 'square' shaped projection patterns (closed dotted-line, Figure 9C–D, subpanels III) and the medial horizontal projection (Figure 9C–D, subpanels III) were less frequently observed, as compared to control females.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Overexpression of FruMB and FruMC had large phenotypic impacts, whereas FruMA did not.
source: Overexpression of FruMB and FruMC had large phenotypic impacts, whereas FruMA did not, consistent with previous functional studies of the FruM isoforms (Nojima et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Overexpression of FruMB resulted in a higher frequency of the 'M' shaped projection pattern in males.
source: Overexpression of FruMB resulted in a higher frequency of the 'M' shaped projection pattern in males (curved dotted-line, 'M'-like, Figure 9E–F, subpanels II), while the 'U' shaped SEG projection was not observed as frequently ('U'-like, Figure 9E–F, subpanels IV).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Overexpression of FruMB causes the 'U' shaped SEG projection to not be observed as frequently in males.
source: Overexpression of FruMB resulted in a higher frequency of the 'M' shaped projection pattern in males (curved dotted-line, 'M'-like, Figure 9E–F, subpanels II), while the 'U' shaped SEG projection was not observed as frequently ('U'-like, Figure 9E–F, subpanels IV).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Overexpression of FruMB causes the density of the neuronal projections in the AbG to be reduced in males.
source: The density of the neuronal projections in the AbG was also reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: In females, overexpression of FruMB causes the lateral ascending neuronal projection in the VLP region to be observed more frequently.
source: In females, the lateral ascending neuronal projection in the VLP region is observed more frequently (Figure 9E–F,III).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: The overexpression of FruMC led to substantial reduction of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α intersecting neurons in both males and females.
source: The overexpression of FruMC led to substantial reduction of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α intersecting neurons in both males and females (Figure 9G–H, subpanels III), which could be due to a loss of neurons and/or their projections.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: The phenotype due to FruMC overexpression could be due to reduced DIP-α-Gal4 expression, given overexpression of FruM was previously shown to reduce expression of some IgSFs.
source: The phenotype could also be due to reduced DIP-α-Gal4 expression, given overexpression of FruM was previously shown to reduce expression of some IgSFs (Dalton et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic perturbation experiments and citation to previous work.

claim: A loss of the FruMC isoform, only in fru P1 neurons, had less strong phenotypic consequences.
source: A loss of the FruMC isoform, only in fru P1 neurons, had less strong phenotypic consequences (fruFLP/ fruΔC; Figure 9I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: In males, loss of the FruMC isoform causes the SMP projections to appear more female-like.
source: In males, the SMP projections appeared more female-like and there was an increase in neurons with a lateral projection, due to loss of the FruMC isoform.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Overexpressing FruMC isoform in the broad DIP-α-Gal4 pattern impacts fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons more substantially than loss of FruMC isoform in only fru P1 neurons.
source: Therefore, overexpressing FruMC isoform in the broad DIP-α-Gal4 pattern impacts fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons more substantially than loss of FruMC isoform in only fru P1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of genetic perturbation experiments.

claim: The wildtype FruMC spatial expression pattern is critical for function.
source: This suggests that the wildtype FruMC spatial expression pattern is critical for function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic perturbation experiments.

claim: Overexpression of FruMC could interfere with other Fru isoform functions, since all Fru isoforms have a BTB domain thought to mediate dimerization.
source: It is also possible that overexpression of FruMC interferes with other Fru isoform functions, since all Fru isoforms have a BTB domain thought to mediate dimerization.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on protein structure and genetic perturbation experiments.

claim: Overexpression could titrate out co-transcriptional regulators leading to larger impacts.
source: Furthermore, overexpression could titrate out co-transcriptional regulators leading to larger impacts.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on genetic perturbation experiments.

claim: If we limit the overexpression of TraF and FruM to only fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons using an additional transgene (tub>GAL80>), we also see phenotypes that are less severe than observed when overexpression is in all DIP-α neurons.
source: If we limit the overexpression of TraF and FruM to only fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons using an additional transgene (tub>GAL80>), we also see phenotypes that are less severe than observed when overexpression is in all DIP-α neurons (see Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments and reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Quantitative and spatial changes in the expression of sex hierarchy genes alters the sexually dimorphic fru P1 ∩ DIP-α patterns.
source: Overall, quantitative and spatial changes in the expression of sex hierarchy genes alters the sexually dimorphic fru P1 ∩ DIP-α patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic perturbation experiments.

claim: Sex differences in morphology are downstream of sex hierarchy regulation, through both cell autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms.
source: This demonstrates that sex differences in morphology are downstream of sex hierarchy regulation, through both cell autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic perturbation experiments.

claim: Out of the 36 genotypes screened, only one perturbation robustly alters the fru P1 ∩ DIP expression pattern.
source: Out of the 36 genotypes screened, only one perturbation robustly alters the fru P1 ∩ DIP expression pattern (Source data 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi and over-expressor screen.

claim: Knocking down DIP-ε in all DIP-α neurons changes the fru P1 ∩ DIP-α pattern.
source: Knocking down DIP-ε in all DIP-α neurons changes the fru P1 ∩ DIP-α pattern (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Males show a significant loss of neuronal projections that have 'U' shaped arbors when DIP-ε is knocked down in all DIP-α neurons.
source: Males show a significant loss of neuronal projections that have 'U' shaped arbors (see Figure 10C, subpanel I).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Both males and females show a reduction of a set of descending neurons when DIP-ε is knocked down in all DIP-α neurons, compared to control flies expressing RFP RNAi.
source: Both males and females show a reduction of a set of descending neurons when compared to control flies expressing RFP RNAi (see Figure 10C, subpanel II).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Females show an enhancement of projections in the SMP region of the brain when DIP-ε is knocked down in all DIP-α neurons.
source: In addition, females show an enhancement of projections in the SMP region of the brain (see Figure 10C, subpanel III).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: These enhanced SMP projections have longer and more extensive projections that are not observed in males.
source: These enhanced SMP projections have longer and more extensive projections that are not observed in males.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: No other dpr or DIP RNAi perturbation shows the three phenotypes observed with DIP-ε knockdown, suggesting that they are specific to the DIP-ε perturbation.
source: Given that no other dpr or DIP RNAi perturbation shows these three phenotypes, this suggests that they are specific to the DIP-ε perturbation (Source data 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: No obvious morphological changes are observed in the ventral nerve cord when DIP-ε is knocked down.
source: No obvious morphological changes are observed in the ventral nerve cord.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Males no longer show a significant reduction of the 'U' shaped projections when DIP-ε RNAi knockdown is limited to only the fru P1 ∩ DIP-α co-expressing neurons.
source: Males no longer show a significant reduction of the 'U' shaped projections, and neither sex shows a significant reduction of descending neurons (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments with restricted expression and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: Neither sex shows a significant reduction of descending neurons when DIP-ε RNAi knockdown is limited to only the fru P1 ∩ DIP-α co-expressing neurons.
source: Males no longer show a significant reduction of the 'U' shaped projections, and neither sex shows a significant reduction of descending neurons (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments with restricted expression and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: The loss of 'U' shaped projections and descending neurons phenotypes are due to reduction of DIP-ε outside of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons, in a non-cell-autonomous manner.
source: This suggests that these phenotypes are due to reduction of DIP-ε outside of fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons, in a non-cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of RNAi knockdown experiments with different expression patterns.

claim: Females still have the enhanced projections in the protocerebrum when DIP-ε RNAi knockdown is limited to only the fru P1 ∩ DIP-α co-expressing neurons.
source: Conversely, females still have the enhanced projections in the protocerebrum.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments with restricted expression and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: The enhanced projections in the protocerebrum phenotype is cell autonomous and driven by a reduction in DIP-ε expression inside the fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons.
source: This suggests that this phenotype is cell autonomous and driven by a reduction in DIP-ε expression inside the fru P1 ∩ DIP-α neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of RNAi knockdown experiments with different expression patterns.

claim: Both fru P1 ∩ DIP-α and DIP-ε are expressed in similar patterns in the SMP.
source: The results are consistent with the observation that both fru P1 ∩ DIP-α and DIP-ε are expressed in similar patterns in the SMP (Figure 3) and so it is not unexpected that expression of DIP-ε RNAi can have a functional impact in fru P1 ∩ DIP-α.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 3.

claim: DIP-ε plays a critical role in establishing wildtype fru P1 neuronal patterns, in both a cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous manner.
source: Taken together, these results suggests that DIP-ε plays a critical role in establishing wildtype fru P1 neuronal patterns, in both a cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: dprs/DIPs are regulated by FruM and expressed in fru P1 neurons in both males and females.
source: Based on our reevaluation of previous genomic data sets and the microscopy results presented, we show that dprs/DIPs are regulated by FruM and expressed in fru P1 neurons in both males and females (Figures 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reanalysis of genomic data and immunofluorescence analyses.

claim: A reanalysis of five genomic studies showed that nearly all the dprs/DIPs are found in at least three of the fru P1 analyses.
source: A reanalysis of five genomic studies showed that nearly all the dprs/DIPs are found in at least three of the fru P1 analyses (Goldman and Arbeitman, 2007; Dalton et al., 2013; Neville et al., 2014; Vernes, 2015; Newell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by reanalysis of genomic data.

claim: The expression pattern for each fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP genotype is unique.
source: The expression pattern for each fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP genotype is unique, although many genotypes have expression in the same brain regions, including the lateral protocerebral complex, mushroom body, antennal lobe, tritocerebral loop, mesothoracic triangle, and abdominal ganglion (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 7.

claim: Many genotypes have expression in the same brain regions, including the lateral protocerebral complex, mushroom body, antennal lobe, tritocerebral loop, mesothoracic triangle, and abdominal ganglion.
source: The expression pattern for each fru P1 ∩ dpr/DIP genotype is unique, although many genotypes have expression in the same brain regions, including the lateral protocerebral complex, mushroom body, antennal lobe, tritocerebral loop, mesothoracic triangle, and abdominal ganglion (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analyses and reference to Figure 7.

claim: These regions were previously shown to be among those with the most pronounced sexual dimorphism in fru P1 neurons.
